abstract: M. Benjamin (Associate Member) (contributed) : It appears to be a feature of all the test results shown that the most violent fluctuations of deceleration occur immediately after the drum comes to rest. As a matter of fact, that is a feature of sharp braking generally-on trains and cars, for example. The bump that throws you out of your seat often occurs just as the speed reaches zero.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The President : About two years ago, one of our assistant engineers experienced a rather disturbing occurrence. He reported that he had been travelling in a cage when the hoist tripped out. Although the hoist had been travelling relatively slowly, the decleration was such that he was thrown on to the floor of the cage. We studied the winder circuits and the braking system but could not find a suitable explanation. We, therefore, borrowed from our friends of the Goldfields their Cambridge decelerometer, and tried to reproduce these conditions. One of the authors and two other officials got into the cage with the Cambridge decelerometer ; they were travelling at a relatively slow speed and, after two or three tests, which were quite innocuous, the driver did something which reproduced the original conditions. The author was thrown on the floor, and the other two passengers fell on top of him. After that, it was decided that engineers, in spite of popular opinion, are not expendable, and that steps must be taken to find an instrument suitable for doing in safety the routine and experimental tests which are required to prove what hoists will do under all circumstances. The result of these decisions is the instrument you have seen demonstrated to-night.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: THE PRESIDENT : We believe that over the years many frills have been added unnecessarily to the electrical systems of winders. This stemmed largely from the selling set-up wherein the large firms supplying electrical equipment had close financial arrangements on tendering. Once there was no financial competition the rivals competed by the inclusion of frills. As an example there were prior to the war, many and various controlled electrical braking systems. These have exercised our ingenuity over the years in devising how to get rid of them. Amongst the frills, however, there have been many sound advances in the art which have proved their worth. I suppose we must countenance the inclusion of frills otherwise we should not achieve the advances, the difficulty is to assess whether an innovation is an advance or a frill. In many cases practical experience only can determine this.

abstract: J. K. GILLETT (Member) : From an academical point of view, Mr Hunter's paper has several interesting features ; as a serious contribution to the methods suitable for getting us out of our difficulties with regard to power shortages, I find it singularly unsatisfying. The most glaring omission, of course, is the amazing lack of figures or curves to show why centralized load control should ever be resorted to. If it is decided to instal such a system, how much is it going to cost for capital and maintenance charges, and what benefit is it going to be ? There is nothing in this paper to induce a hard-pressed municipal electrical engineer to coax a large sum of money from his Council to purchase such a load-control device ; I am given to understand that for a moderately sized town, an injector costs about 7 000 and each relay about 5 plus the erection and maintenance charges, but I contend that the actual savings to be effected are ephemeral.

articleTitle: A telemetering instrument for the measurement of acceleration and deceleration of mine hoists
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This paper describes an instrument developed in South Africa which, while measuring the apparent change of gravitational forces inside the conveyance in a mine shaft, transmits these quantities electrically along the winding rope to the surface, from where they are transmitted to the engine room, interpreted automatically and recorded as the actual acceleration and deceleration of the conveyance. The description of the instrument is followed by a discussion on test results which indicate the accuracy and usefulness of the apparatus for mechanical and electrical braking adjustments and for the investigation of winding problems generally.

articleTitle: The activities of the power and communications systems co-ordinating committee during the period may 1941 to july 1952
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This report deals with the activities of the committee during the period since its previous report made in November 1941. Details are given of the preparation of a directive on separating distances between power and telephone routes. Data is supplied on low-froquency induction with particular reference to South African conditions. The problem of the noise induced into telephone lines at power-route crossings is treated. The value of power transpositions in reducing noise induction is discussed. The general noise situation in South Africa is reviewed and several interference problems, which the committee intend to investigate in the near future, are mentioned.
